tripwire.my_view: Good design, not a trap, but under-signposted. Its purpose is to make a REPAIR visible: once U0.22/U3.2/U6.16/U6.17 are fixed, the frozen exemption claims keys the handoff no longer lacks, and the correct act is to delete that entry AND update the pin -- which is exactly the two-visible-edits property the pin exists for. The trap risk is real because the tempting shortcut (loosen the check, or re-derive the baseline from live data) would re-absolve every recorded gap, which is the flaw class U8.25 just removed. On the live corpus the test computes over={} (constant during this unit, 170 handoffs, no mid-write exclusions), so it is not vacuous and not currently red.
tripwire.remedy_self_evident: Not yet self-evident. The message names the harm ('the exemption would silently tolerate the key being lost again') but not the remedy. One clause would fix it: 'REMEDY: delete this baseline entry and update BASELINE_GAPS_SHA256/VERIFIER_BASELINE_SHA256 in tests/test_orchestration_handoffs.py -- do NOT loosen this check and do NOT re-derive the baseline from live data.' A matching comment beside the pin constants would make the two-edit ritual obvious at the point of failure.

red_green.detail: On the SAME one-newline tamper of state/logs/U8.18/verifier_shape_baseline.json: the NEW guard fails byte-exactly (verbatim message above). The OLD guard has NO U8.18 sha pin at all and its only U8.18 checks (pre-image :232-235) are json.loads(file) compared to an inline copy and set(list) == set(frozenset(list)) -- a trailing newline cannot change either parsed value, so all three of those assertions pass on the tampered file. That is verified by source inspection of the whole pre-image, not by a live replay: my replay harness aborted on a bug in my own driver (NameError before the exec), so the old-guard half is a source-level proof, not an executed one. The executed half of the same property is the U8.15 cycle, where the old guard DID carry its own byte-exact pin (BASELINE_GAPS_SHA256 = 9b0b0a71...) and bit on a one-byte change: 'U8.15 frozen baseline changed: 6929e34f...'. So the old guard was byte-exact for U8.15 and byte-blind for U8.18; the new guard is byte-exact for both.

overrun_judged.evidence_for_or_against_guard: Both, and it is worth separating them. FOR the guard's value: handoffs are machine-read (170 of them, plus the frozen baselines), and the one defect this unit class exists to prevent is a handoff nobody can parse -- the very defect U8.15 was created for. Eleven calls spent recovering its own JSON is exactly the cost the guard is meant to make impossible to ship; a self-inflicted recovery is strictly cheaper than a downstream machine-read failure. AGAINST its ergonomics: the churn was avoidable and the guard had nothing to do with it. Nothing in the guard requires a 20 KB JSON to be hand-authored in one write with no validation step; a json.dumps-based writer or one validate-after-every-edit pass (which I ran at STEP 0 and after the final write) collapses that loss to zero. Verdict: evidence FOR the guard's necessity, AGAINST the unit's authoring discipline -- a weaker guard would not have saved those 11 calls, and a better writer would have.
